newsitem.title: USA: Clinton helped with "nudge in the right direction.
newsitem.headline: Clinton helped with "nudge in the right direction.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday that he hoped a "little nudge in the right direction" from him to representatives of United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union helped them reconcile their differences.

As he celebrated his 51st birthday on vacation here on the island of Martha's Vineyard, the president made a subtle claim for some of the credit for coaxing the opposing sides into a tentative deal to end a 15-day UPS shipping strike.

On his arrival at Martha's Vineyard on Sunday night, Clinton had summoned a television reporter to say he had a "gut feeling" the two sides would settle. Holding two fingers together, he said, "They're that close."
But in a pointed warning to the Teamsters that they should not take public support for granted, Clinton had said, "Right now, the Teamsters have public sentiment, but that will turn."
At the time, the two sides were expressing optimism but warning the negotiations could just as easily collapse into a new round of accusations and recriminations.
About 24 hours after Clinton made his comments, the two sides reached agreement.

Asked about his intentions on Tuesday, Clinton told reporters the strike's endgame reminded him of negotiations between the White House and Congress when the two sides are close to a deal but need a push.

"Sometimes you get very close and you've got 95 percent of the issues resolved, and maybe just a little nudge in the right direction helps you get over the top, and I was just hoping to do that," he said.
He added: "They did the work and they deserved the credit. They resolved their differences in a way that I think was good for the company and good for the employees."
White House spokesman Barry Toiv said Clinton felt it had been an appropriate time for him to speak up after keeping silent during most of the walkout.

"He felt that at that point in the process the best role he could play was to continue to encourage them to show optimism and by doing that help keep them at the table and working to reach an agreement," Toiv said.

Throughout the drama, the White House resisted appeals to mediate, insisting the walkout did not endanger the country's health and safety, the conditions for intervention under the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947.
In the last days, however, Labor Secretary Alexis Herman raised the stakes by coaxing the two sides back into the negotiating room and sitting in on some of the talks.

Clinton had special praise for Herman, saying she "did a very fine job in working with the parties, trying to keep them working together and getting back together. I know that she deserves and will get some much needed rest today."
